narrative: The model estimated a 56.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is slightly above a coin flip, not a certainty, but because admission here is tied to this risk estimate, your application was rejected. The single most influential factor was your LSAT score of 36, which is just below the accepted-student average of about 37. In this case, that factor leaned toward passing. The decision was tipped the other way by the next two factors. Your third-year class rank decile of 2, far below the accepted average near 5.8, was the second most influential factor and pushed strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.50, below the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure. Together, these academic signals outweighed the LSAT’s favorable signal and produced the predicted failure risk. To strengthen a future application, focus on the areas that drove this decision: take additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate/pre-law program to improve your academic record, prepare carefully and retake the LSAT if possible, and provide a clear addendum explaining any circumstances behind your rank and GPA along with a concrete study plan. Seek admissions advising before reapplying.
